So I'd put to you that when you're speaking of territorial ethnic changes, you're speaking of changes in the makeup of Serb-claimed territories that were being reported to you and to the other members of the Presidency. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I say there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30944 receives number P6667, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6667 is admitted. Mr. Traldi, if you're moving to another subject, I think we are close to the time where we would take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think it's an excellent time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, we will take a break of 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 10 minutes past mid-day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a late start due to technical problems, which seem to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi and me are using body language because we are trying to fit into today's schedule to finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually it's the Chamber to be blamed for it, but now it's really technical problems that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get LiveNote up and running before we start, but I think we will be able to share the remaining time basically evenly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to hear that the Chamber doesn't need to encourage you to pay proper attention to this issue, because if the witness could leave today, before the weekend, that would be good, or at least during the weekend and not to stay over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have 65 ter 30946.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This will be an interview published in Belgrade Borba, an interview with you, in which you discuss territorial ethnic changes of the sort that we were discussing before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have page 2 in the English and the top of the far right column on page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you zoom in, please? I can't really read. It's too fine print.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The top of the far right column for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you read it now, Witness, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it's the right column, middle of the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you're asked: "Do you have a personal position on the criteria according to which that split should be carried out?" And you answer: "In my opinion, only two criteria are possible. One is for the split to be carried out in accordance with shares in the national structure of the population. In other words, for each people to receive approximately as much territory as the percentage that it represents in the total number of inhabitants of BH. The one who has a third of the population cannot claim two-thirds of the territory or vice versa. Or, since there are three constituent peoples, the criterion may be that the total territory should be divided into three approximately equal parts. The Serbs would receive approximately the same thing under both criteria, while the Muslims and Croats would fare very differently in one case or the other." So my first question: This refers to dividing the control of territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina on an ethnic basis; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Second, as I understand it, you're suggesting here that the RS, the Bosnian Serbs, should have been entitled to approximately one-third of the land, whichever of those criteria was applied; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 4 in the English, and looking at the box on the bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S, bottom centre, we see the heading, "Aggressors and aggressors," a little lower on the page in the B/C/S than where we are now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, could you check if we have the right portion in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We don't yet. Could we zoom out for a moment? And it's where it says at the very bottom centre, "Agresor i agresor."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You're asked a question here: "If the Serbs are not the aggressors as they claim in contrast to the world, then how can one justify the fact that they have used weapons to conquer more than two-thirds of the territory in spite of the fact that they only have one-third of the population in BH?" Now, you were aware that Bosnian Serbs were claiming two-thirds of the territory at this time; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had under their control about 70 per cent of the territory, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this is as of August 1992. Now, you answer: "The problem is that in BH, neither the first side nor the second nor the third has shown any willingness, either in peace or war, to respect any sort of principles of justice, tolerance, respect for the interests of others, et cetera. Just as in parliamentary competition, i.e. in the political phase, the Muslims and Croats did not shrink from abusing their numerical superiority to outvote the Serbian side, the Serbian side did not shrink from using its advantage in heavy weapons in wartime conditions." And that's right, isn't it, that the Serbs had used their advantage in heavy weapons throughout the months leading up to August 1992 when you gave this interview?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, owing to that, they actually placed under their control 70 per cent of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Those are the territories from which, in the Bosnian Serb Presidency, you'd received -- or sorry, in the Bosnian Presidency, you'd received reports that there were territorial ethnic changes occurring because of violence and war and genocide; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That 70 per cent of the territory you just mentioned, that's the territory where, when you were in the Bosnian Presidency, you received reports that there were territorial ethnic changes occurring because of violence and war and genocide; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those reports did not show the situation in the Mostar valley where the situation was reversed, where the Serbs were victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question, I think. Could you please answer the question? You were shown a little time ago part of the minutes of a meeting in which you said something, and the question now is whether the 70 per cent you mentioned a minute ago is about territories, as you said in that meeting, that they were ethnically changed or the ethnic changes were occurring because of violence and war of genocide, whether you were talking about approximately the same territories. Or at least those 70 per cent to be included in what you said during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And by this point you'd been in Belgrade for two months; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Meeting with Serb officials in the SFRY government, like President Cosic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This continued to be your opinion as to what was happening on the ground in Bosnia, didn't it? The Serb side was using its advantage in heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Actually I have a couple more quotes to show you from the article and I'll ask it then. At the end of the paragraph that we are looking at, you say: "With respect to the territorial ambitions of the Serbian side, double its share in the national structure of the population, it is strange that people are keeping silent about the fact that today we have completely symmetrical conduct on the Croatian side. Naturally both are equally unacceptable." Your view was that Serb and territorial -- sorry, Serb and Croat territorial claims were both unacceptable; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please read the quote, the part that you're quoting, through the end so that my point can be clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think I did. It reads: "With respect to the territorial ambitions of the Serbian side, double its share in the national structure of the population, it is strange that people are keeping silent about the fact that today we have completely symmetrical conduct on the Croatian side. Naturally both are equally unacceptable." And what I asked you was: It was your position then, wasn't it, that Serb and Croat territorial claims in Bosnia-Herzegovina were unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 3 in the English and page 2, left-most column in the B/C/S, you're asked at the bottom of the page in English, and the middle of the left column in the B/C/S, under "Everyone in his own crowd": "Then you do not believe in the proclaimed return of all the refugees as a countermeasure to the partially implemented ethnic cleansing" --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Only on the left column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's the top quote, you can see "etnicko ciscenje" in the B/C/S. So I've read the question. You respond: "Unfortunately, I think that there will be much" --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me finish your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need the right portion on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is -- yes. And the witness is apparently not able to follow it. Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you see the first question you're asked under: "Svako svome jatu [phoen]"?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that's the question I read out a moment ago, isn't it? You have to articulate your answer for the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you could read it one more time because I wasn't able to follow earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Happy to do it. "Then you do not believe in the proclaimed return of all the refugees as a countermeasure to the partially implemented ethnic cleansing." And you answer: "Unfortunately, I think that there will be much more territorial and ethnic concentration during the upcoming peace than was done in this regard by war operations, destruction, and expulsions." And it was your position at the time that the ethnic concentration that had occurred up to this point had been caused by war operations, destruction, and expulsions; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you said earlier you'd been in Belgrade for two months at this time, you'd been meeting with Serb officials in the SFRY, senior officials, that remained your position as of this time, end of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 18097?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is another interview you gave around the same time. I'll be looking for the third and fourth paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I noticed that in the English translation, names are mentioned again and again where they appear not to be in the original. Now, could you -- not in this one but the previous one. Could you carefully check that there are no other new elements introduced? You see it's always Vucinic, Kecmanovic. Now, it may well be that it's explained in the beginning but it certainly does not appear in the original text, and therefore that always raises some concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I believe the names you've mentioned are the interviewer and the interviewee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No doubt about that, but apparently someone has been editing rather than just translating.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We are happy to have it reviewed, if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least check carefully that that's the only thing and then I take it that there is no major problem, is there? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As to this interview, at the first -- at the top it says Presidency member resigns and we are talking about you here, you'd resigned by the end of August 1992 from the Izetbegovic Presidency; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Looking at the third and fourth paragraphs, we read: "The process of dismembering of Bosnia-Herzegovina along its ethnic seams within the internationally recognised territory has gone beyond the point of return, Kecmanovic said on Monday night, explaining the reasons for his resignation. The Muslim Bosnia, the Croatian Herceg-Bosna, and the Serbian Republic are territorially defined entities with a population ethnically homogenised by force." By that point, large areas of the Republika Srpska had indeed been ethnically homogenised by force, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only by force, but by fear as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 18097.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18097 receives number P6668, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6668 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask that the previous document, 30944, be marked for identification and we'll review it as you've suggested, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Kindly check the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm told that what I meant was 30946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that at this moment I made an observation in relation to that one. I expect the Prosecution to carefully look at it, but it's not a reason at this moment not admit yet. But I leave it open that the parties can revisit, if it turns out that there is more edited than just the names of the interviewer and the interviewee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm in your hands in that respect, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you tender it, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30946 receives number P6669, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6669 is admitted into evidence. And of course I expect the parties to revisit it pretty soon if there is any reason to do that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now to finish this topic, sir, in paragraph 55 of your statement, you speak about the movement of populations and you say it was possible, you believe, to transform Bosnia and Herzegovina territorially and ethnically without any radical or forced changes to the ethnic structure on the ground. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Whether or not it was possible, based on your statements at the time, that's not what happened, is it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some official proposals, but they were all rejected by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I'd put to you that in your statement, you're saying it was possible to do this when you know, and you said publicly at the time, that what actually happened was that the ethnic composition of Bosnia was transformed in a completely different way, through violence, through war, through genocide. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, the last question, you didn't answer the question, but you thought it more important to give the reasons why you think it didn't happen, and even did not answer the question itself. Could I please ask you again to focus on the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the Vance-Owen Plan. I'm going to move through it very quickly. I know you're aware of a great many details so I'm going to make an effort to put to you the key details and ask you to confirm them. The plan was based on the idea of a central state of Bosnia with a number of regions; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, to the extent I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was an attempt to preserve a sovereign multi-ethnic state?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was initially met with some reluctance by all three warring parties?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In April 1993, Slobodan Milosevic was pressured to support it and he in turn pressured the Bosnian Serb leadership to support it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Bosnian Serb Assembly met about it in early May 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And General Ratko Mladic, the commander of the Bosnian Serb Army, forcefully demonstrated during the Assembly deliberations the amount of land the Serbs would have to give back as part of the plan, and it was then rejected; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any details of the Assembly discussion. I do know that the plan was rejected by the Serbian Assembly, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 1D02002? This is the witness's expert report in the Simic case. And I'm looking for page 41 in the English, 38 in the B/C/S, paragraph 82. I think we may have a different page in the B/C/S. If we could go back three pages. Now we have the right page in the B/C/S, and if we could get page 41 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you -- you wrote this expert report yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And reading at the end of the paragraph, we see: "The latter," that refers to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, "meeting on 5 and 6 May, voted overwhelmingly against ratification of the Vance-Owen Plan. On this occasion, as before, it was the map that constituted the biggest problem for the Serbs, something that General Ratko Mladic, the commander of the Bosnian Serb Army, forcefully demonstrated during the Assembly deliberations. In a referendum held on 15 May, the Bosnian Serbs decisively rejected the plan which was now truly dead." Does this refresh your recollection as to whether General Mladic made such a speech at that Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And do you stand by what you've written here, that after that speech, the plan was rejected?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to intervene here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not the proper presentation of the evidence. It's not after the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it was after in time, it was after, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After in time, yeah, but it's after my birth as well, so it's not my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it is -- first of all, whether it's -- let me first -- if this should be understood as an objection, then it's denied. So could you please first answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to be precise, please. Could you read out the sentence in question? On that occasion as previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Witness, you should first answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you can see the sentence. Do you stand by your evidence as reflected here?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so it's right, isn't it, that after General Mladic's speech on this occasion, the Vance-Owen Plan was rejected?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, it says that he gave a speech at the Assembly session. It says that the Assembly rejected it. And it says that then, ten days later, or nine days after the end of the session, the Bosnian Serbs decisively rejected the plan. You stand by all those things; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have in mind the specific issue of General Mladic. In my report, it is only stated that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Witness, let me stop you there. What we see happening is that a text is put to you, that apparently Mr. Lukic has some concern as whether the Chamber would consider a chronology as a causal relationship. Now, this Chamber is able to make a distinction between time and causality. That's one. Second, whether there is any causal relationship, the Chamber of course will consider that. What Mr. Traldi does is that he points to certain fact which, I take it, Mr. Traldi, you would consider relevant to establish such a causal relationship, and you're not distancing yourself from such a causal relationship, you're only referring to time, but of course there is some suggestion in that. The Chamber is fully able to cope with that, so neither the witness nor the parties need to have any further concern about the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you stand by he gave a speech, after that speech the Assembly voted it down. On the 15th, the Bosnian Serbs decisively rejected the plan. That's all true, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let us stay with the text precisely. I didn't write here that following his speech, the Assembly voted it down. Or rather, that his speech changed the tone of the Assembly. That's not what one can read from here. On that occasion, the map was a problem as it had been previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are doing exactly what I asked you not to do: To be concerned about this Chamber not knowing the difference between causal relationship and chronology. Therefore, you demonstrate now again that you either have not understood me or that you do not wish to understand me. Simply, do you stand by the referendum held on the 15th of May decisively rejecting the plan, which was now truly dead, by the Bosnian Serbs? Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If formulated the way you put it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you stand by on the 5th and the 6th of May, that there was an overwhelmingly -- vote overwhelmingly against the ratification of the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you stand by the fact, as written here, that the map constituted the biggest problem for the Serbs and that General Ratko Mladic, the commander of the Bosnian Serb Army, forcefully demonstrated that during the Assembly deliberations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: To just briefly look at the causal issue, I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play one more clip. And this has been given 65 ter 22466A. We have not had the transcript confirmed in this case. We just had it made. So we may need to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need to play it twice. Mr. Kecmanovic, that's for purposes of verification of interpretation. So you'll see it twice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "RM: We have to show to all those present the current situation. Not everyone can see it from up close like we soldiers can. "MB: When we saw those maps, Milosevic and I looked at each other. We couldn't understand what he was talking about. "RM: It shows the results achieved by our leadership, our people and our army. "BP: It was so clear when he presented two maps. There was a factual map and a transparent map showing the Vance-Owen proposals, showing the current situation in the field. It was very visual. And the delegates could see how much territory the Serbs would get by the Vance-Owen Plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, first, that's the speech you were describing in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Ms. Plavsic's reaction reflects the importance of General Mladic's speech in it those deliberations; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 22466A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but in front of me on paper I have only B/C/S version and here, on the titles, I read, under line 7, "victorious." There is no such a word in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: To preserve the time for both of us and ensure we finish today, I'd be happy to have it MFI'd and talk to Mr. Lukic at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It will be MFI'd. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22466A receives number P6670, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6670 is marked for identification pending further consultation between the parties. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to my last topic now which is your departure from Sarajevo. Aside from you and Mr. Pejanovic, was there also a Serb named Simovic who had remained part of the BiH government?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there for a while but he too left Sarajevo later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He told you in June of 1992 that there were messages from Pale that you Serbs who remained in the BiH government should leave your posts in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we've agreed, at that time, it would have been advantageous for the Republika Srpska government if the Serbs who were in the Bosnian government departed. You'd agree with that; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my opinion. You mentioned the conversation involving Mr. Koljevic at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction -- interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly repeat the end of his answer because he trailed off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think you need to repeat your answer after saying I mentioned the conversation with Mr. Koljevic. The interpreters couldn't hear the rest.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Koljevic's call and his conversation with my family suggesting that I do not become a member of the Presidency. Nevertheless, I did. And as I used my judgement at the time, I relied on it again when I left. It was on my own, of my own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to test that evidence. Before we do, you agreed with me, I think, when I mentioned that phone call from Mr. Koljevic, that it was a public relations problem for him, for the RS government, that you and other Serbs remained part of the Izetbegovic government; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think the conversation took place at the time I was invited to join the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right. That would have been a month earlier. I had put to you at the time --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- that he'd told your wife it would be a detriment to the Serb people for you to join the government. And you agreed with that. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd put to you, when we were discussing it, that that was because it would be a public relations problem to have Serbs in what would then appear to be a multi-ethnic, inclusive, Bosnian national government. I'd put it to you again now.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that it was their interpretation. That it was their opinion. It certainly wasn't mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 30941, page 144?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This will be another part of your Krajisnik testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I don't yet have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's on its way. I can see that on the screens before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I lack your foresight, I'm afraid, but it is here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was put to you: "Well, Professor, I don't want to split hairs about particular people and the reasons they may have entered or remained for a particular period of time, but in the political situation of that moment when the Bosnian government wanted -- was presenting itself as a unitary multi-ethnic government and the -- and Republika Srpska wanted to repudiate or denounce that position, it was advantageous if the Serbs who were in the government departed. Correct?" And you started your answer by saying: "Yes, you're right. That is correct." And then you explained a particular event. Do you stand by your testimony in the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have that text translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But you heard it through your ear-phones; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want it to be read again because there is no B/C/S version of this. There is, but there is an audio which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please read it again, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was put to you -- I'll focus on the critical part of the question if that's all right. "... in the political situation of that moment when the Bosnian government wanted -- was presenting itself as a unitary multi-ethnic government and the -- and Republika Srpska wanted to repudiate or denounce that position, it was advantageous if the Serbs who were in the government departed. Correct?" And your answer reads: "Yes, you're right. That is correct." My only question for you at the moment is: Do you stand by your Krajisnik testimony as truthful?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, soon after the conversation you had with Mr. Simovic, in early July 1992, you arranged with Mr. Izetbegovic to go to Lukavica and then to Pale to meet with the Bosnian Serb leadership; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You had to make arrangements because in early July, it wasn't possible to move out of Sarajevo freely; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This had been the case since early May; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, could we have 65 ter 02451? These are the minutes of the 14th session of the Republika Srpska Presidency. It's held 3 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's just before you left Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 in both languages, item 12 is a conclusion that: "Mr. Kecmanovic, Mr. Pejanovic, Mr. Simovic, Mr. Nikolic and other Serbs shall be publicly invited to withdraw from their positions in official bodies of the Republic of BH or to publicly renounce their role as representatives of the Serbian people in those organs." Do you see that text?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 02452? These are the minutes of the 15th session of the Republika Srpska Presidency. This session is held 6 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's around when you left Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I'm particularly interested in item 3 for which we need to turn to the bottom of page 2 in the English and to page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This indicates that Dr. Koljevic and Momcilo Krajisnik were appointed to talk to you, Professor Kecmanovic, and determine conditions for your resignation. And it says that in order to resign, you should present certain demands to Mr. Izetbegovic. Do you see that text?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to item 4, on page 3 in the English, still on page 3 in the B/C/S. It's actually just -- it's point 4 in item 3, so I think I may have confused matters slightly by how I labelled it, but it's at the top of the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "The Serbian Republic of BH shall amnesty, protect, and enable all those who resign from the Muslim-Croatian leadership to leave the Serbian Republic of BH." You see that text as well; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have a few questions about this document. First, it's correct that after you left Sarajevo, you met with both Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also met with other members of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Those included Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Aside from them, you did, just for the clarity of the record, meet with Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in fact, you told them about the situation in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they talked to you about the situation around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it's correct that after those talks, you went by helicopter to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were offered to go with Mr. Karadzic immediately but you went the following day in a helicopter with Mr. Koljevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So the Bosnian Serb government enabled you to leave the Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was agreed in Sarajevo at the Presidency. It was agreed that I should go both to Pale and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you never went back to the Izetbegovic Presidency, did you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Soon afterwards, you did resign, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So after the document we've just seen was issued, you did meet with the people appointed to negotiate with you, they did enable you to leave Republika Srpska, and you did resign. That's all true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation that is announced here, with the conditions that were presented, such a conversation with Krajisnik and Koljevic did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. That was not the question. Did you meet with those? I think you confirmed that already. Did they enable to you leave the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you resign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have one final exhibit. But before I pull it up, it says here the Serbian Republic of BH shall amnesty those who resign from the leadership; right? At point 4?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. No one said anything of that nature to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 01737E? Once the transcript comes up, I'll ask Ms. Stewart to play the audio. This is part of a conversation between General Mladic and President Karadzic recorded on the 2nd of December, 1995, and Mr. Karadzic is speaking at the end of the portion that's been redacted on this page. The transcript continues to a second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the same issue as far as audio or video is concerned. Now, of course, if there is no disagreement among the parties on whether this reflects the original audio, then of course we could just do it by reading which is -- this is an official translation, I take it, it's not just --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I didn't do it myself, no, Mr. President. It's an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to that extent, of course, it has been verified already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's true, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic? But officially of course our interpreters are interpreting from audio and not -- so therefore the same rationale still applies. Let's hear it twice to be consistent in our approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. I'm not getting anything either so I might just read the relevant portion if that's more suitable. I know we are pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please read it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be played again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Karadzic: I mean ... it's that little Stankovic, let's say, their man. "Mladic: And who is Stankovic? "Karadzic: Stankovic, don't you remember going back to ... he was in the leadership as well ... "Mladic: I don't know. Which Kecmanovic, that buffoon of ours who was in ... "Karadzic: No. "Mladic: ... with Alija? "Karadzic: Yes, yes. If someone says 'join the Presidency,' he would join the Presidency. But the greatest shame -- the greatest disgrace for him, he's politically dead because -- because of that ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The audio was very unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we're missing actually the line I was looking for at the end in what was just read back from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way to play then again the last, well, let's say, 10 or 15 seconds?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Mladic: They granted him asylum in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's what is described in the previous document as well, right, that members of the Izetbegovic government who resigned would be given asylum?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever said anything to that effect to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my examination. I have the last three documents to tender. That's 02451, 02452, and 01737E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2451 receives number P6671. Document 2452 receives number P6672. And document 1737E receives number P6673, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6671, 72, and 73 are admitted into evidence. We take a break, Witness. Mr. Kecmanovic, we would like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I will not be able to finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll not be able to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously. But then -- so we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With so many documents, probably at least two full sessions. I'm ready to stay longer today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we have -- the Chamber may have problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask, since we cannot contact the gentleman, that somebody from the VWS asks him if he can stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or informs him that and asks --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe -- because we were told -- we fixed his testimony for yesterday and today. Maybe he has some obligations on Monday, so then we will have to organise his return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could well be. Madam Registrar, could you take care that Victims and Witnesses Section informs the witness that most likely we will not conclude today and that therefore his availability over the weekend and on Monday should be enquired.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and then under those circumstances, let's take a break of 23 minutes. We resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will wait for a second for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Earlier I said that the Chamber could not continue to sit this afternoon. Now, there are many, many problems in doing that. One of them, if I understand you well, Mr. Traldi, that you are -- you couldn't stay, which the Chamber fully accepts. The other matter is that the Chamber would have to sit 15 bis because I'm not available this afternoon. Third, we would need further assistance, we do not know whether the interpreters will be available because we can't require just interpreters to stay here forever. So that is further explored. So there are many, many, many reasons. Then of course we have Mr. Mladic. If Mr. Mladic says: It's just too much for me, we have agreed on a certain court schedule, then we will accept that. If he says: I want to be present, I want to attend, and this is too much, we will fully accept that. So there are many, many reasons why we would not continue to sit. However, if all these reasons are resolved, then of course we would consider that. Now that takes some time. At least 10 to 15 minutes, to find out. But let's go with the simple matters first. What if we would have two more sessions this afternoon, would that be agreed to by Mr. Mladic, because if not, we will not do it. Mr. Lukic, could you -- have you discussed the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think there are other preconditions, but Mr. Mladic says if Mr. Kecmanovic has to leave, he will try to be with us for two more sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that's -- and then perhaps we should take a bit of a longer break so that -- okay. That problem seems not too prohibitive for further hearing the case this afternoon. Prosecution, I do understand Mr. Traldi has to leave. It's quite unusual to replace counsel, but I would like to hear from the Prosecution whether under the present circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, we wouldn't stand in the way of continuing, Mr. President. And I appreciate your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the second problem resolved. The third problem, and I have to address my colleagues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I convey to everyone that my colleagues would not oppose against sitting, as we call it, 15 bis this afternoon if I would not be present. That's the third problem resolved. Then the last one is whether we have sufficient support staff, interpreters, security, I do not know. We need the full team at -- court reporter as well. That's -- of course the court reporter is included in the full team. And I think it would take us some -- at least a couple of more minutes to find out whether that would be possible. Now, at the same time, I know that one of the Judges has -- still has a question for the witness, which preferably is put to him before the re-examination starts. Therefore, I am inclined to ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom so that at least he can answer that question, and hopefully, at the end of this, I could inform him about the results of Madam Registrar trying to compose a full team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, as you've heard, the re-examination will take considerable time, more than the 15 minutes we have available. I also do understand that you reported not to be available on Monday. Therefore, every effort is made to see whether we could continue this afternoon. It's highly uncertain whether that's possible, especially support staff might be the problem. So therefore, at this moment we do not know whether we will continue this afternoon or whether you would have to be recalled at a later stage, and that could not be the end of July because then we -- the court is in recess. It would then be late August or early September for further re-examination. Of course, we are trying to avoid that but that's how the situation is at this moment. However, before we finally determine that matter, Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you which you're invited to listen to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, I have to take you back to your testimony yesterday. On page 23862, you talked about detention facilities for Serbs in Sarajevo in two hotels, Hotel Zagreb and Hotel Europa. How often did you visit this detention facility in Hotel Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice. I went twice to Hotel Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you describe the detention facility you saw there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not enter the Zagreb hotel. I went there asking that the people who were being held there be released. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means you didn't visit the centre itself?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually entered the hotel itself but not their cells. I didn't go to the rooms where they were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you talk -- did you see the people who guarded the detainees?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were they in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some had military police uniforms, others civilian police uniforms. Then there were uniforms from the reserve force of both the military and police. And some had some kind of passes, referred to in some of the documents we saw yesterday. At one Presidency session, there is some discussion about those passes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not interested in any Assembly session. I want to know what you saw. To which army belonged the military police people?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say. There were people without any uniform there as well. With these passes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the military police you mentioned first.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were supposed to belong to the military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To which army did they belong?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of BH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you see any insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many of those have you seen?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the detention facility itself or you mean in general?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Of course I'm only talking about the detention facility.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where was this detention facility in the hotel located?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hotel basement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go to the basement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where was the detention facility in Hotel Europa located.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was only in the basement or in some other premises as well. I went up to the reception desk of the hotel asking that they be released. I was looking for specific detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you enter the detention facilities itself?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can now give the final report, Mr. Lukic, and please listen very carefully. It will be possible to have one session this afternoon, which could be a 75-minute session, after a break. You would have ten minutes until now. If you think you can manage, then we would do that. If you think that it would be irresponsible for you, as Defence counsel, to proceed in this way, just tell us and we'll cancel any session this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First, I would like to ask Professor what would be the good time for him to come back, if necessary. And if we cannot finish today, I don't see any point to torture everybody to continue longer. I still could have him back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think you can't finish, we shouldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think I cannot finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is more to be said about all that but we will not do that at this very moment. Then the one and final thing we would have to ask the witness is -- well, first of all, it's -- Monday, you say, it's -- you have to be in Belgrade. Now, we were all willing to accommodate you, to change our schedules, to do whatever we could, and it turns out to be impossible. My question to you is: How urgent, how important, is the matter for you to be in Belgrade on Monday so that you could not, as we all tried to do, consider to change your plans? And to be here on Monday morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is of exceptional importance. I really cannot do it but I would be willing to stay today for as long as needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't help us out. Could you shed any light on exceptional importance? I'm not asking for details, or if you would like to deal with it in private session? If you say in the family there is something very important, that would -- or is it political or is it -- I'm just asking you whether you could give us a bit of an idea of what and how the importance is to be understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are private reasons and I'm not at liberty to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I fully accept that. Then when would you be available in the times to come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned late July as a possible solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not any earlier? I mean, if we are talking about late July, when does late July start for you? Does that start -- it's my recollection that the 24th is a Friday which means 27th is a Monday again. Would you still be available in the week ending the 24th? We are not sitting on the 25th but the 24th then is a Thursday. That week, is that -- falls that within the end of July or? That's the week of the 21st of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I actually meant the very few last days of July, the very last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The court is not sitting then, so therefore then it would be at its earliest late August, early September. Are there any dates you would not be available late August, early September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Late August is an option. But I can only confirm precisely from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I invite you that you communicate with the Victims and Witnesses Section if there are any dates on from, well, let's say, approximately the 25th of August when you would not be available, and -- because you have to communicate now through the Victims and Witnesses Section. You could not communicate with the calling party or -- and we'll try to arrange a new date for further re-examination, late August or in September. Before you leave, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way, not in writing, not -- whatever, about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today and yesterday or whether that's testimony still to be given upon your return. If I said today, yesterday, testimony given until now. Therefore, any communication with this Tribunal should be channelled through the Victims and Witnesses Section. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I wish you, although only temporarily, a safe return home again, but we also hope to see you back in late August or in September. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, before we adjourn, could you ask the Victims and Witnesses Section to take care of a constant channel of communication with the witness, in case they would want to contact him or if he wants to contact the Victims and Witnesses Section?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is one item we could deal with at this moment, but we have -- we need to go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I take it that on Monday you have a witness ready to appear as the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
